The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.

papers.title: Who Shows Up, Who Benefits, and Who Wins? Expert-Novice Disparities in Team-Seeking Forums and Competition Performance on Kaggle
papers.authors: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei
papers.summary: Team formation is the first social gate to collaboration in online communities, yet it remains unclear whether public team-formation mechanisms broaden access to collaborators or reproduce existing hierarchies. We examine this question on Kaggle, a data science competition platform whose "Looking for a Team" (L4T) megathreads let participants publicly seek teammates for on-platform competitions. Grounded in Communities of Practice theory, we conduct two complementary studies of 18 competitions held in 2023. Study 1 analyzes the reply network among 671 megathread participants and finds that 89.3% are low-tier users, yet higher-tier users receive significantly more replies (Kruskal-Wallis H=16.46, p=.00246) and achieve higher rates of forum-visible teaming success (52.9% vs. 32.6%; chi-squared=10.53, p=.001), a proxy for eventual team membership. Linking megathread posters to verified team rosters from 16 competitions partially supports this proxy. Twenty-six final teams contained two or more megathread posters, indicating that megathread interaction sometimes, but not always, maps onto realized teaming. Study 2 links participation traces from 219 users to private leaderboard outcomes and finds that productive participation (submission count rho=.435, cross-competition participation rho=.247) is positively associated with performance, whereas megathread-specific discussion is not (rho=-.021). The submission-performance association appears stronger in higher tiers, although the novice subgroup estimate is imprecise. Together, the findings suggest that open access to team-seeking forums does not guarantee equal participation. Visible expertise shapes who attracts attention, and engagement in the community's core practice is more strongly linked to success than discussion alone. We discuss implications for designing more equitable team formation in online collaboration environments.

papers.title: Robot Demonstration Videos Should Include Transparency Disclosures
papers.authors: Nozomi Nakajima
papers.summary: This paper argues that the robotics and AI community should adopt disclosure standards for demonstration videos. As physical and financial constraints limit direct public access to embodied AI, public dissemination of progress in robotics is mainly through curated demonstration videos rather than direct experience with the technology. In a large-scale (N=9,341), pre-registered experiment across six countries, we find that the general public struggles to discern both the visual authenticity (e.g., distinguishing real footage from CGI) and behavioral authenticity (e.g., distinguishing autonomy from teleoperation) of robot demonstration videos. The omission of these details distorts public perception, leading people to overestimate the ability of robots to perform tasks and navigate real world environments. Using evidence from behavioral science, we design a disclosure intervention and demonstrate that the inclusion of clear disclosures in robot demonstration videos significantly improves discernment of visual and behavioral authenticity, as well as understanding robots' capabilities. We propose the adoption of disclosure standards for robot demonstration videos to accurately calibrate public expectations and promote transparency in robotics research.

papers.title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
papers.authors: Yiting Chen, Kelin Yu, Sarthak Kaingade, Bryan Trinh et al.
papers.summary: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.

papers.title: NVFP4-MLA: Unified FP4 KV-Cache Storage and Attention Computation for Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.authors: Chao Ni, Qi Zhang, Xiao Wang, Zongfei Jing et al.
papers.summary: Long-context reasoning and agentic workloads make key-value (KV) cache capacity and attention computation the dominant costs of serving frontier large language models. We present NVFP4-MLA, the first design to push both KV-cache storage and attention computation of multi-head latent attention (MLA) to FP4. NVFP4-MLA co-designs the quantization algorithm with the attention kernel and the cache system. Selective residual compensation preserves model accuracy by adding NVFP4 residuals only to the quantization-sensitive channels. Two-dimensional quantization blocks make the shared latent cache compatible with the different reduction directions of the two attention batched matrix multiplications (BMMs), removing requantization between them. On DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi-K3, NVFP4-MLA matches BF16 MLA average accuracy across nine benchmarks while compressing the MLA KV cache by 3.20x and 3.05x relative to BF16 MLA. On NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, NVFP4-MLA speeds up the attention kernel over FP8 MLA by up to 2.82x on DeepSeek-R1 and 2.71x on Kimi-K3, and lowers p90 time to first token in agentic multi-turn serving by up to 3.5x and 2.1x, respectively. In disaggregated DeepSeek-R1 serving, it also raises per-GPU throughput by up to 2.30x.

papers.title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
papers.authors: Alexandre Petrachini, Breno Bernard Nicolau de França, Guido Araujo
papers.summary: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.

papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh et al.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

papers.title: From Language-Specific to Cross-DSL: Semantic-Role-Guided Model Completion with LLMs
papers.authors: Meriem Ben Chaaben, Théo Giraudet, Benoit Combemale, Houari Sahraoui
papers.summary: The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs), trained on vast and diverse corpora, has positioned them as a promising source of domain knowledge to assist modelers. However, leveraging LLMs for model completion remains challenging: suggestions must respect both the syntax of a domain-specific language (DSL) and the intended domain semantics, while remaining consistent with an evolving model. This paper presents RAFiC, an LLM-based approach for iterative domain model completion that generalizes across DSLs. It drives completion using metamodel information to ensure syntactic validity and enriches prompts with semantic-role annotations to better capture the intended modeling role of DSL elements. The approach provides context-aware, incremental guidance during model construction. We evaluate RAFiC through an ablation-based comparative study over three DSLs and two scenarios per DSL to isolate the contribution of syntactic and semantic guidance. Across these six scenarios, semantic role guidance improves contribution rate in every case, and RAFiC improves completion effectiveness over weaker prompting configurations in most of them. The largest gains occur for DSLs that are less represented in LLM training data. In these cases, iterative guidance leads to earlier and more stable accepted suggestions, while semantic role guidance improves their relevance.

papers.title: Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
papers.authors: Ruike Lyu, Bolun Xu
papers.summary: We show that co-locating distributed AI servers with industrial demand and coordinating AI workloads with production loads can substantially reduce the additional grid interconnection that AI computing requires. Grid interconnection is increasingly constraining the expansion of large AI data centers. Factories already have grid connections sized for their peak production loads, and we propose hosting AI servers during production valleys. We formulate a joint optimization that sizes CPU and GPU servers, schedules deadline-constrained tasks, and routes tasks among factories, and use it to compare three factory-site architectures with new large data centers serving the same demand. Applying this framework to 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, we find that AI demand and production loads often do not peak together. As a result, AI servers placed at factories and scheduled according to production peaks need about 60% less additional interconnection capacity than new large data centers, and 98% less when tasks are routed among a group's factories.

papers.title: Mining Unity VR Repositories for Refactoring Patterns and Technical Debt
papers.authors: Faraz Gurramkonda, Neeraj RandhirSingh Saini, Michael Gharbieh, Bruce Maxim et al.
papers.summary: Maintaining virtual reality (VR) applications poses challenges tied to real-time performance, hardware dependencies, and complex interactions. Yet little is known about how developers refactor these applications, which kinds of technical debt they address, or how well automated tools capture VR-specific changes. We mined 1,755 candidate refactoring commits from 176 open-source Unity VR repositories and manually examined a sample of 303 commits, of which 270 contained at least one refactoring. We also extended RefactoringMiner to create VRRefMiner, a tool that detects conventional refactorings in C# scripts used by Unity applications. Our analysis found both conventional and VR-specific refactorings. VR-specific changes addressed concerns such as interaction logic, performance, and Unity-specific artifacts. Code debt was the most prevalent category overall, while interaction debt and UI/UX debt were the main categories addressed by VR-specific refactorings. Across the repositories, VRRefMiner detected 15,549 operations spanning 68 refactoring types, with structural moves and extractions accounting for 31.0% of detections. It detected conventional refactorings in 216 of 246 commits labeled as general refactoring. In the 24 commits labeled as VR-specific, the tool could detect conventional changes but identified no VR-specific refactoring categories. These results point to a need for detection techniques that account for both source code and the Unity artifacts involved in VR maintenance.

papers.title: Level Up! AI-Driven Challenges and Adaptations to Code Review Practices
papers.authors: Kaia Newman, Christian Bird, Jenna Butler, Emerson Murphy-Hill
papers.summary: AI can write code faster than humans can review, causing a bottleneck and necessitating changes to code review practices. This bottleneck is hotly debated, giving rise to two extreme and orthogonal imagined futures: one where humans continue to be firmly entrenched in the review process, and one where AI agents merge pull requests entirely without human involvement. Yet, these futures remain rooted in folk wisdom. Through a mixed-methods study of interviews (n = 24) and a survey (n = 2,590) at a large, multinational software company with widespread access to AI, we identify AI-driven code review challenges and strategies reported as effective to meet them. We found that AI enables, necessitates, and complicates a shift in the human reviewer's role toward high-level concerns (e.g., design and intent). We found that AI-assisted authoring results in increased burden for reviewers due to challenges such as a lack of author stewardship and PR volume and size, potentially leading to downstream debt. Our survey showed AI review usage was not correlated with less difficulty keeping up with PR volume, indicating using AI for review alone is not sufficient for solving AI-driven review challenges. Developers found the most useful strategies to be organizations supporting and resourcing review, pushing review burden upstream, and prioritizing reviewer attention on the concerns that matter most.

papers.title: Optimal Operating-Point Selection for Single-Linearization Trajectory Planning of Nonlinear Robot Manipulators
papers.authors: Bhanuka Dayawansa, Rohan Munasinghe
papers.summary: Single-point linearization provides a computationally efficient basis for optimization-based trajectory planning of nonlinear robot manipulators. However, planning performance depends on the selected linearization point. This paper presents an offline performance-driven approach that treats the location of a single linearization as an optimization variable. Candidate operating points are sampled from a common cubic seed trajectory, and each corresponding affine model is used to solve an identical constrained finite-horizon quadratic program (QP). The resulting control sequences are executed on the original nonlinear dynamics, and the operating point minimizing the nonlinear trajectory objective is selected through grid search and bounded refinement. Evaluation on four point-to-point motions of a three-degree-of-freedom UR5 manipulator yields optimal normalized operating-point locations between 0.325 and 0.935, demonstrating trajectory-dependent selection. Compared with the best-performing conventional initial, midpoint, or terminal linearization, the proposed approach reduces the nonlinear trajectory objective by 17-18%, 21-22%, 37-38%, and 7-8% across the four tasks, respectively. Additional nonlinear execution with identical PID feedback correction confirms that the performance advantage persists for a representative task. These results demonstrate that systematic operating-point selection can substantially improve single-linearization trajectory planning while preserving a fixed affine planning model.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Clustering Algorithm and Parameter Selection for Collaborative Population Stratification Using Distributed PCA
papers.authors: Maryam Ghasemian, Lynette Hammond Gerido, Erman Ayday
papers.summary: We propose a privacy-preserving selection layer for collaborative population stratification workflows, enabling an honest-but-curious server to recommend a strong clustering algorithm-hyperparameter configuration from privacy protected shares. Instead of using a fixed workflow such as PCA followed by K-Means with a preset number of clusters, the framework compares multiple clustering methods and parameter settings under privacy constraints. To avoid relying on a public reference basis, we construct a shared low-dimensional representation through a distributed-PCA (DPCA) procedure in which each party computes local top-r principal-component information and the server aggregates only low-rank summaries to recover a global basis. Building on this representation, the framework supports three LDP-protected pipelines: PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, and Noise-Only. The server evaluates clustering methods and parameter settings using internal validation metrics and recommends a top-performing configuration from the perturbed data; this step is pure post-processing. Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes show that the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong settings from LDP-protected data. Across both datasets, the PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, and runtime, and show lower membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets. Overall, they provide the best utility–scalability trade-off in our setting.

papers.title: Dependable Voice Command for Multi-UAV Swarms Using Small Language Models
papers.authors: Afshin Ameri, Luiz Giacomossi, Håkan Forsberg, Ivan Tomasic et al.
papers.summary: Supervisory control of multiple autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) imposes high visual and cognitive demands on human operators, particularly when communicating mission objectives and system constraints. Voice command provides a natural interaction modality that can reduce operator workload; however, its reliability is affected by environmental noise, speech variability, and recognition errors. This paper presents a dependable voice command framework for multi-UAV swarm supervision using Small Language Models (SLMs). The proposed architecture integrates an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) module with an SLM-based semantic processing layer to transform spoken operator commands into structured task definitions for downstream multi-UAV planning and execution. To evaluate robustness, an end-to-end assessment pipeline is developed using a Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) to generate synthetic supervisory commands, which are converted into audio samples with varying operator accents and environmental signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). The resulting speech signals are processed by the ASR module, and the SLM performs contextual interpretation and phonetic correction of transcriptions when required. The evaluation isolates the resilience of the voice command pipeline under acoustic degradation and speech variation, demonstrating reliable task generation for multi-UAV supervision in challenging operational conditions.

papers.title: Correcting Persistent Failures in Point-Cloud Grasping Policies using Human Demonstrations in Virtual Reality
papers.authors: Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Karthik Rengarajan, Bharath Narasimhan, Chris von Csefalvay
papers.summary: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.

papers.title: Memory Safety Isn't All You Need: Code Reuse Attacks in Memory Safe Languages
papers.authors: Eric Cornelissen, Musard Balliu
papers.summary: Memory safety rules out classical code reuse attacks that rely on arbitrary memory corruption, but does not eliminate code reuse altogether. Attacks such as object injection, prototype pollution, class pollution, DOM clobbering, and DOM script gadgets arise in memory-safe languages without violating the underlying memory safety abstraction. We show that these seemingly different attacks share a common structure: Attacker-controlled data influences accesses to shared runtime state, such as runtime type information, prototype or class state, and the DOM, and a value fetched from that state subsequently influences a security-sensitive operation. Drawing on this insight, we develop a language-agnostic framework that decomposes an attack into a weakness, ending in a fetch from shared runtime state, and a gadget, which propagates the fetched value to a sensitive sink. We show that the framework captures five established attack classes and use it to derive stateless, mutating, and recycling weaknesses, together with simple, vertical, and horizontal gadget structures. We further systematize existing defenses into three common strategies - mediation, minimization, and constraint - and use them to derive candidate defense directions. Finally, we develop a model language that gives a formal account of code-reuse weaknesses and potential conditions for gadgets and end-to-end vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Quantifying Membership Inference Risks in Genomic Data Sharing: The Role of Attacker's Auxiliary Information
papers.authors: Maryam Ghasemian, Lynette Hammond Gerido, Erman Ayday
papers.summary: Genomic data sharing is essential for biomedical research but introduces significant privacy risks, including membership inference attacks, in which an adversary determines whether a specific individual's data was used in a study. Existing privacy protections are typically applied after a release format has already been chosen, leaving researchers without a principled method to assess dataset-specific risk beforehand. We propose a server-assisted, principal component analysis-based pre-release auditing framework that maps genomic data into a shared low-dimensional space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with a formally derived sensitivity for principal component analysis scores, and estimates membership inference attack power at a controlled 5% false-positive rate using a distance-threshold attack. A membership-neutrality diagnostic based on Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness is reported alongside attack power, precision, and recall. Experiments using the openSNP and 1000 Genomes Project datasets across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the researcher's dataset and public auxiliary data in principal component analysis space is a dominant determinant of attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone. Comparison against a genome-wide association study-style likelihood ratio test baseline further contextualizes the measured risk. This framework enables researchers, data repositories, and institutional review bodies to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risk before genomic data publication, supporting more informed and privacy-aware biomedical data-sharing decisions.

papers.title: Lightweight Replay Attack Detection via Interpretable Physical Descriptors
papers.authors: Saba Nasiri, Alireza Amirshahi, Milos Cernak
papers.summary: This paper proposes a lightweight, interpretable audio anti-spoofing method that distinguishes between bona fide human speech and replay attacks by analyzing physical acoustic signatures rather than learned spectro-temporal patterns. Unlike black-box Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), our approach exploits fundamental physical invariants, specifically source kinematics, binaural phase dynamics, and aerodynamic consistency, captured via multi-channel microphone arrays. By extracting these explicit physical descriptors and classifying them with an efficient XGBoost model, we achieve detection performance (Equal Error Rate (EER) of 17.8% on 6-channel arrays) comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning baselines, but with a fraction of the computational cost. The proposed system operates with a 1 MB memory footprint and 0.9 s latency on a standard ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller, enabling privacy-preserving, real-time liveness detection on edge devices.

papers.title: Revisiting Re-executability: Coverage-Guided Symbolic Feedback to Improve Decompilation
papers.authors: Yuxin Hu, Xiaohan Wang, Kevin Leach
papers.summary: When source code is unavailable, decompilation provides a source-level representation of a binary. However, code recovered by conventional or LLM-assisted decompilation may not preserve the original behavior of the binary. Recent approaches evaluate re-executability using fixed test suites, but passing these suites does not ensure behavioral preservation. We present SymDec, an LLM-assisted decompiled-code repair system that uses the original binary as a behavioral reference. SymDec uses coverage-guided symbolic execution to explore the I/O-level behavior of the original and recompiled binaries, and symbolic comparison to identify inputs that expose behavioral differences. These inputs are replayed on both binaries to confirm the differences, which are returned as structured feedback to guide subsequent LLM revisions. We evaluate SymDec on 120 functions from ExeBench and DecompileBench, compiled for x86-64 and ARM64 at optimization levels O0-O3, yielding 960 binary decompilation tasks. More than half of the tasks yield candidates that pass the supplied test suite and complete symbolic comparison without detected behavioral differences. Among candidates that pass all supplied tests, symbolic comparison exposes replay-confirmed behavioral differences in 4.5% of cases, showing that test-suite re-executability can miss behavioral discrepancies. Under the same input-generation budget, symbolic execution achieves higher mean line and branch coverage than black-box fuzzing. Symbolic feedback also improves the conventional metric, increasing the mean single-step test-pass rate from 90.1% to 93.3%. These results show that symbolic comparison provides stronger evidence of behavioral consistency than test-suite re-executability alone and supplies effective feedback for repairing decompiled code.

papers.title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
papers.authors: Shervin Shahidi, James Poon, Hang Xie, Kenneth O. Xu et al.
papers.summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus 4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, p=0.002) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, p=0.004); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.

papers.title: We Have All the Cards: Securing Agent Cards at the Operational Trust Boundary of the Agent2Agent Protocol
papers.authors: Miguel A. Guirao Aguilera, Satyajayant Misra, Efren Lopez-Morales
papers.summary: AI agent interoperability protocols enable orchestrators to discover and invoke external agents using machine-readable metadata. In the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, Agent Cards contain attacker-controllable natural-language fields that may influence agent selection before a provider is invoked, creating a pre-invocation trust problem. We characterize this discovery-time attack surface through a taxonomy of ten Agent Card manipulation attacks and present SECCARD, a layered validation framework combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM-based semantic reasoning. We measure the emerging public A2A ecosystem by probing 36.1 million Internet domains and collecting 310 deployed Agent Cards. Two annotators independently label the corpus with 96.8% agreement. We then construct a 660-card real-card perturbation benchmark with matched benign controls and a 260-card synthetic adversarial benchmark spanning all ten attack categories. On controlled attacks injected into real Agent Cards, the strongest semantic judge achieves 97.0% security recall at a 1.7% false-positive rate. Across nine LLM judges on the synthetic benchmark, security recall ranges from 25.8% to 92.3%, demonstrating substantial model-dependent variation. These results show that SECCARD effectively identifies Agent Card manipulations spanning all ten discovery-time attack classes while preserving benign Agent Cards, but also reveal that its effectiveness depends critically on the choice of the underlying LLM judge.

papers.title: Passage-Focused Soft Coordination for Hierarchical Multi-Robot Navigation in Bottleneck Environments
papers.authors: Haoze Dong, Stepan Dergachev, Meng Guo, Konstantin Yakovlev et al.
papers.summary: In multi-robot navigation, rigid global schedules are sensitive to execution deviations, while local methods lack long-horizon coordination. We propose a passage-focused framework combining soft global coordination with flexible local execution. A passage-induced graph of convex sets supports priority-ordered planning with two levels of soft coordination. Passage-aware route selection accounts for passage usage and traversal directions, while route-restricted continuous space-time planning penalizes temporal conflicts. The resulting references guide a model predictive path integral controller that avoids collisions online. Adaptive temporal and geometric tracking accommodates execution deviations, while selective replanning maintains coordination without rigid trajectory reservations. Across 1,200 instances in 4 different environments with 5-30 robots, the framework achieves a near-perfect success rate and outperforms evaluated baselines in makespan and flowtime. Hardware experiments with 8 robots demonstrate successful completion of all trials without collisions. These results highlight the effectiveness of passage-focused coordination in balancing long-horizon cooperation with flexible execution.

papers.title: Stargate: Security Analysis and Mission-Aware Firewall for the CubeSat Space Protocol
papers.authors: Owen Ramsey, Carlos Gonzalez-Cortes, Efren Lopez-Morales
papers.summary: The CubeSat Space Protocol (CSP) is widely used for communication in CubeSat missions, yet its security model and attack surface remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present a systematic security analysis of CSP and identify fundamental limitations in its trust assumptions, coarse-grained network abstractions, privileged management services, application command semantics, and lack of mission-context awareness. Based on these findings, we develop a taxonomy of CSP attacks spanning four classes: network identity abuse, management service abuse, application semantic abuse, and mission context abuse. We then introduce Stargate, a modular, mission-aware firewall that enforces CSP-specific policies derived from this taxonomy, including node and service authorization, command-level filtering, and mission-context constraints. We implement Stargate and evaluate it on a virtual testbed based on a real-world CubeSat mission and flight software. Stargate successfully blocks all 11 representative attacks across the four attack classes while introducing only 1.42 ms of additional median round-trip latency. Our results demonstrate that protocol- and mission-aware policy enforcement provides a practical approach for securing CSP-based spacecraft networks.

papers.title: Technical Report of Auriga's 1:10 Scale Autonomous Vehicle Robot
papers.authors: Marya Sabouri Dodaran, Ali Taheri Garakani, Mandana Shabanzadeh Nasrollah-Abadi, Yousef Ashrafi et al.
papers.summary: This report presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle, developed at Shahid Beheshti University's Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory. The platform integrates a custom mechanical chassis, a distributed embedded system based on ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX module for high-level perception and control. The embedded layer manages sensor interfacing, real-time data acquisition, and actuator control, while the Jetson handles environment perception through deep-learning–based lane, sign, and traffic light detection, as well as decision-making and trajectory control. System communication is achieved via structured UART links, ensuring synchronized operation between perception and control subsystems. The vehicle's software stack incorporates ROS, modular firmware design, and multiple control algorithms—Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit—to achieve stable autonomous navigation in structured driving scenarios. The overall system demonstrates robust performance and reliability in urban-like environments, serving as a modular research platform for future autonomous driving studies.

papers.title: eDIAR: Training-Free Open-Speaker Streaming Diarization for Long Meetings and Large Archives via e-means
papers.authors: Kyudan Jung, Jihwan Kim, Minwoo Lee, Eunji Shin et al.
papers.summary: Meetings last up to an hour, and nobody knows in advance how many people will speak. Neural diarizers with a fixed number of output slots, such as Streaming Sortformer and Nemotron-3, are accurate and run online, but they cannot name more speakers than they have slots. We remove this limit without retraining. The slot head keeps deciding who is active and when speech overlaps, and speaker embeddings are clustered inside a single slot, with the official e-means algorithm, only after every slot has been used. In the streaming system, re-clustering is confined to a bounded window, labels are revised for a few seconds, and identities are anchored to the slots of the head. The resulting system has no limit on the number of speakers and stays accurate when speakers outnumber the slots, where fixed-slot models break down. On meetings that grow to an hour it stays far more accurate than Streaming Sortformer, which accumulates errors, and its cost per update does not grow with the meeting. The same recipe turns the four-slot Streaming Sortformer into an open-speaker system. Across recordings, e-means makes it affordable to link the speakers of a large archive frame by frame, a task that arises when conversational corpora are prepared, and it reaches the clustering quality of Lloyd's k-means several times faster. The method needs little tuning, and e-means runs with its default recipe from a few hundred to more than a million embeddings.

papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.authors: Jianjun Ou, Matthew Lentz
papers.summary: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

papers.title: Voice-Based Conversational Agents as AI Care Assistants: Evaluating Personalization, Intervention Delivery Fidelity, and Privacy Expectations in Older Adults' Care
papers.authors: Thalia Viranda, Shupeng Wang, Jia Bo, Yuchen Yang et al.
papers.summary: Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. This shift creates two challenges: how to personalize support while faithfully delivering evidence-based interventions, and how to manage personal-data use and sharing across AI and care stakeholders. We designed and evaluated ARC, a voice-based conversational agent that operationalizes multidomain lifestyle intervention through sessions with predefined goals, participant context, and evidence-based components. In a 3-day remote study, 80 older adults completed 473 sessions across six session types (9,183 turns; averaging 19.4 turns and 6 minutes per session). Participants reported favorable usability, acceptability, and use intentions. System-level analyses showed strong domain-level but modest participant-specific contextual reuse, no significant personalization-fidelity association, and fidelity limitations centered on incomplete delivery of intervention components rather than off-protocol drift. Within care relationships, expectations for personal-data use and sharing varied by data type and recipient. Our findings support feasibility of conversational delivery of multidomain lifestyle intervention, offer methods and system-design insights for longitudinal evaluation, and motivate an evaluation agenda for generative AI health interventions: user-experience and outcome measures should be complemented by evidence of whether intended intervention processes were delivered as designed.

papers.title: DIRT: Depth-completed Image-based Rendering using Two-band Blending for Live Novel-view Synthesis
papers.authors: Mathias Harrer, Laura Fink, Noah Lewis, Paul Himmler et al.
papers.summary: State-of-the-art novel-view synthesis (NVS) methods commonly require per-scene optimization before rendering, limiting their applicability in live settings. Live or ad-hoc NVS, however, demands low-latency rendering during capture and strong generalization to new scenes. Some previous work tried to address this task by adapting training- and optimization-based methods, trading quality for low latency. We introduce a live NVS approach following traditional image-based rendering that operates on a posed set of depth sensor observations and images. Our method leverages explicit, sparse point-based geometry obtained from active sensors, resulting in a sparsely filled depth buffer that is completed in the (novel) target view's screen-space. Using this proxy, a posed set of images is projected into the target frame before fusing the resulting observations through a frequency-aware two-band blending strategy. The pipeline is entirely non-neural and optimization-free, requiring no training data or scene-specific optimization. As a result, our approach reduces the delay between capture and novel-view rendering and does not rely on favorable network generalization. We validate the method's applicability to heterogeneous sensor setups - including handheld RGB-D cameras, automotive LiDAR, and thermal cameras - as well as challenging scenarios, such as low light captures. Our experiments demonstrate that the approach outperforms prior methods in live reconstruction scenarios, while maintaining competitive performance in conventional NVS benchmarks.

papers.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
papers.authors: Solano Amadori
papers.summary: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.

papers.title: BPU-SpikeMM:Exact Matrix Multiplication via Spatio-Temporal Spike Encoding on Real Neuromorphic Hardware
papers.authors: Rongyuan Guo, Yufeng Zhang, Haotian Wang, Canming Yao et al.
papers.summary: Matrix multiplication is the dominant computational kernel in deep learning, yet its growing scale strains conventional von Neumann hardware in energy efficiency and bandwidth. Neuromorphic architectures offer a promising alternative, but mathematical equivalence between matrix multiplication and spiking computation does not guarantee direct execution on real neuromorphic hardware, as the specific hardware paradigm may still require additional data recovery, bit-weight reconstruction, or state readout after neuromorphic execution. This paper presents BPU-SpikeMM (Brain Processing Unit-based Spike Matrix Multiplication), an exact spatio-temporal spike encoding framework for matrix multiplication on real neuromorphic hardware. We prove the exact equivalence of spike-encoded matrix multiplication under the BPU execution paradigm, distinguish mathematical equivalence from native direct-readout equivalence on BPU hardware, and build a spatio-temporal offloading pipeline supporting multiple encoding schemes. Furthermore, we extend the framework to a multi-dimensional encoding design space and evaluate the applicability of different encodings on real BPU hardware in terms of correctness, temporal resource cost, spatial resource cost, and event-driven metrics. The results confirm native direct-readout equivalence across all evaluated encoding schemes and show that their applicability to BPU execution depends on joint trade-offs among temporal cost, spatial resource consumption, and event activity.

papers.title: TetraCoder: Adaptive Tetrahedral Encoding for Neural Fields
papers.authors: Daniele Della Pietra, Antonella Rech, Nicola Conci, Nicola Garau
papers.summary: Implicit and explicit representations of geometry are central in computer graphics applications and come with their pros and cons. With surface sampling being faster on explicit representations and spatial queries being faster on implicit representations, finding efficient conversions between them is a highly desirable property. We present TetraCoder, a single resolution hash-free adaptive tetrahedral encoding that links an explicit tetrahedral spatial encoder with an underlying implicit signed distance field (SDF). The resulting hybrid implicit-explicit space is continuous piecewise affine (CPWA) by design, allowing to obtain an exact correspondence between the implicit SDF and the explicit analytic mesh. TetraCoder's design comes with additional perks, in particular: (a) it scales better than multi-resolution encoding methods due to its single resolution optimizable grid, (b) unlike hash-based methods, it is not affected by collisions, (c) it enables fast tetrahedral ray-tracing, geometry and appearance editing, directly through its adaptive tetrahedral scaffold. We demonstrate the versatility of TetraCoder by showing an improvement over state-of-the-art methods on multiple tasks: 2D/3D fitting from images and point clouds, 3D novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction, and geometry/appearance editing.

papers.title: Pose-based Neural Clothing for Animated Characters
papers.authors: Julian N. Heidenreich, Vinicius C. Azevedo, Jakob Buhmann, Lento Manickathan et al.
papers.summary: Traditional garment simulation for animated characters is a time-consuming bottleneck for artists due to slow simulations and tedious parameter tunings.Recent data-driven methods offer a powerful alternative, capable of learning from a dataset of simulated data to generate high-quality deformations. A lightweight network design allows data-driven systems to achieve a real-time inference speed. This significantly improves the artist workflow, as they can interactively pose a character and see high-quality folds and wrinkles at animation time, thereby allowing to make creative decisions ahead of time. However, existing neural clothing methods have presented appealing results on datasets based on realistic human models ( SMPL), but when trained on animated character datasets, they struggle to generalize to unseen poses. In this paper, we aim at designing neural networks and training strategies to generalize better to unseen poses in real-time to enable the interactive posing applications. We focus on a production-oriented setting where the model is trained for a single garment in a quasi-static setup. Technically, we leverage a smooth, expressive latent space by first training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We then progressively train the VAE encoder to transition from reconstruction to pose-driven prediction. To guide this prediction, we condition the network on both low-dimensional pose parameters and character body surface displacements. Finally, we introduce a novel local gradient histogram loss that mitigates the over-smoothing effect of reconstruction losses. Extensive evaluations on production-level assets and public datasets demonstrate that our method produces sharp, realistic wrinkles, smooth large-scale drape, and temporal coherence in real-time, offering a robust and easily integrable solution for interactive posing workflows.

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.authors: Mateusz Wozniak, Qi Gao, Agnieszka Wykowska
papers.summary: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

papers.title: Who sets the consent signal? Platform defaults and crawl coverage in measuring opt-outs from AI training
papers.authors: Marcin Lawenda
papers.summary: Web data used in social research and in the training of AI models increasingly carry consent signals, but who sets these signals is rarely measured. This paper attributes opt-outs from AI training to the party that set them. The complete lists of Polish, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian and German domains recorded by Common Crawl, with 3,445,751 reachable sites, were crawled in October 2026 together with a random sample of 10,000 Slovak registry domains. Each signal was matched against vendor templates and identical files. Four exploratory hypotheses were examined with logistic models. Between 0.70% and 3.82% of the listed sites opt out. Platform and hosting defaults set 15% to 78% of the opt-outs. Settings active by default reach 60% to 95% of a vendor's sites, while settings that owners switch on reach at most 2.1%. Most of the higher Czech and Slovak rates compared with Germany are statistically attributable to platforms. Lists derived from Common Crawl miss about a third of the Slovak opt-outs because they exclude sites that block its crawler. The results describe delegated consent, a signal that a platform sets on behalf of its users, which measurements of consent on the web must consider.

papers.title: Go under Chinese Rules with a Succinct Game History is Complete for Exponential Space
papers.authors: Markus Bläser, Felix Czerner
papers.summary: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too. The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.

papers.title: Any Channel Count, One Token Stream: Incorporating Spatial Audio Understanding and Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models
papers.authors: Yuhuan You, Wenxiang Guo, Zhifang Guo, Yuxuan Wang et al.
papers.summary: Audio phase relations encode source locations, yet existing large audio-language models (LALM) reduce audio to single-channel content to stabilise general audio understanding, leaving spatial information for direction, distance, and source-relation questions unused. We present SpheraAudio, which accepts recordings with any channel count – mono, stereo, First-Order Ambisonics (FOA), or higher – and maps them into a single token stream. A spatial encoder turns complex multichannel spectra into spatial tokens interleaved with audio tokens at corresponding temporal positions. Spatial Multimodal RoPE (SMRoPE) makes each token's modality identity and temporal slot visible to rotary attention without altering the language model's original RoPE. Training runs in three stages – spatial-encoder pretraining, projector alignment, and joint supervised-and-reinforcement learning – progressing from geometric supervision to language-based spatial decisions, with answers trained as explicit spatial chain-of-thought: step-by-step geometric reasoning over the heard scene. Current benchmarks tie questions to a fixed channel-count format and score answers without spatial reasoning evidence. We introduce SpheraQA, which spans mono, stereo, and FOA recordings and organises questions hierarchically from single-attribute perception through cross-source relations to multi-step reasoning, scored programmatically against simulated scene geometry and real-recording annotations with step-by-step solution references. Across SpheraQA and public spatial-audio benchmarks, SpheraAudio sets a new performance standard for spatial audio understanding. It supports high-precision localisation, tracking, and reasoning over static and moving sound sources while preserving strong general-audio capabilities. We will release code, SpheraQA, and evaluation metrics to support reproducibility.

papers.title: Reproduction of Simulated Acoustics Scenes Using Acoustics Room Transformer for speech intelligibility tests in Clinics
papers.authors: Ali Fallah, Kirsten C Wagener, Pascal Pflueger, Steven van de Par
papers.summary: An Acoustic Room Transformation (ART) method is proposed for clinical applications to render simulated acoustic environments using six loudspeakers in a reverberant room. In typical clinical settings, testing rooms are not acoustically treated and only a limited number of loudspeakers are available. The ART approach enables control of the playback-room reverberation, allowing speech intelligibility tests to be performed under realistic and perceptually compensated conditions. The method focuses on the two most common Speech Reception Threshold (SRT) configurations: S0N90 and S0N90. One front and one side loudspeaker reproduce the direct sound components, while the remaining four loudspeakers (two in front and two behind the listener) generate the reverberant sound field. The direct sound is optimized in terms of energy, and the reverberant field is adjusted based on both energy and interaural coherence. An additional direct-sound gain is applied to match the clarity index (C50) of the reproduced signals to that of the reference target. Results from speech intelligibility tests demonstrate that, with ART processing, the reproduced scenarios achieve SRT values very close to those of the reference signal in both S0N0 and S0N90 conditions and therefore allow for comparable speech test results independent of the particular test room acoustics.

papers.title: What a Memory Preview Cannot Tell You: Ambiguity in AI Memory Permissions
papers.authors: Sadia Noman Tonni, Nafis Fuad Shahid
papers.summary: A memory rule states when an assistant may reuse a remembered event, and an editor can confirm a rule by previewing one use it allows and one it blocks. We ask what such a preview lets a person infer about the rule they saved. For an editor with six or twelve valid rules, we enumerate every rule compatible with a preview. Splitting the rules most evenly does not target the question a user cares about. For an explicit preference, two adaptive tests leave all three recommendation scopes open (for a one-off choice the outcome turns on a tie), while one test of transfer to another task settles the question. Weak previews are also the default. Under the intended rule, 36 of 39 possible allowed/blocked pairs contain a blocked example that no rule allows, and no pair identifies the rule. Three or four tests suffice here; when permissions depend on each other, a fixed checklist grows to six or nine and adaptive questioning needs at most five or seven. These counts use a specified rule vocabulary and fictional events. In a small pilot, 10 of 20 people who saw such a weak preview of a rule they had just chosen mispredicted, or were unsure about, at least one of two uses, and none of those 10 said the outcomes matched what they wanted. Whether better previews help people is untested.

papers.title: Alleviating Interview Stress: Effects of Robot Persona and Reactive Backchanneling on High-Pressure Mock Interviews
papers.authors: Haochen Yang, Zhuoran Gao, Geqing Tao, Yusi Dong et al.
papers.summary: High-pressure job interviews induce anxiety and impair performance. Existing mock training suffers from a trade-off among cost, standardization, and physical presence. This study investigated how a robot interviewer's verbal persona (supportive vs. challenging) and nonverbal backchanneling (active vs. negative) affect users' psychological states and facial expressions in a simulated interview. In a 2x2 between-subjects experiment (N=28), participants interacted with a NAO robot. Subjective measures (state anxiety, self-efficacy, social presence) and objective facial emotion recognition were collected. Results showed that a supportive persona reduced task load, increased perceived robot warmth and mind perception, and decreased perceived surveillance and robot discomfort. Active backchanneling increased non-neutral (p = .021) and anxiety-tension facial affect (p = .048). A significant interaction effect between persona and backchanneling was found on social presence (p = .045). The subjective-objective consistency was 67.9%, indicating complementary measurement modalities. The findings provide preliminary support for the social buffering hypothesis in human-robot interaction.

papers.title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
papers.authors: Xingyi Li, Jiahao Yang, Yiqin Zhu, Jingwen Ye et al.
papers.summary: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

papers.title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
papers.authors: Takeshi Onishi, Hiroya Makino, Takahiro Yamaguchi, Hiroyuki Sakai
papers.summary: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

papers.title: Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions
papers.authors: Andrew Liu
papers.summary: KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, K state-action pairs and effective horizon H. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability C≥ 4, every estimator needs Ω(KCH³/(εε,β)) samples on some instances when ε is small, where β is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when β≥ 1.4H. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as H/β; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in 1/ε, with no coverage assumption. For β≥ H the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in 1/ε. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.

papers.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
papers.authors: Eilam Shapira, Alan Arazi, Shoham Grunblat, Roi Reichart
papers.summary: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

papers.title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
papers.authors: Jiaxin Huang, Chengxing Lin, Xiaoyu Luo, Sirui Chen et al.
papers.summary: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

papers.title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
papers.authors: Galen Andrew, Arun Ganesh
papers.summary: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability (δ) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small δ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor α> 1. We prove a closed-form bound B(α) < 1 on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that B is log-convex so that the optimal α is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of 1/B(α*).

papers.title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
papers.authors: David Herrera-Poyatos, Cristina Zuheros, Carlos Peláez-González, Andrés Herrera-Poyatos et al.
papers.summary: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.

papers.title: Where to Predict in Retinal OCT? Anatomy-Guided Target Selection for I-JEPA
papers.authors: Yunchu Feng, Wai Tak Lau, Kaveri A. Thakoor
papers.summary: Self-supervised learning aims to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data, potentially allowing models to capture subtle anatomical variations across patients and reduce the amount of labeled data needed. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) learns by predicting target-region representations from visible context rather than reconstructing pixels. However, its uniform target placement does not account for the anatomical structure of retinal OCT, where retinal tissue occupies only part of each B-scan. We investigate anatomy-guided target selection using image intensity and predicted retinal segmentation while retaining the I-JEPA architecture and latent prediction objective. We compare anatomy-guided rectangular targets, anatomy-shaped targets and coverage-constrained placement with uniform masking, and evaluate the learned representations using linear probing for glaucoma classification on FairVision. We found that rectangular targets guided by image intensity achieved the highest linear-probe AUC in our comparisons. We show that anatomically meaningful target selection is promising for retinal OCT representation learning, while greater anatomical specificity did not consistently improve performance.

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
papers.authors: Shiye Su, Xiaohan Wang, Ludwig Schmidt, Serena Yeung-Levy
papers.summary: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

papers.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
papers.authors: Aleksandr M. Shtraukh-Adamsky, Vladimir M. Adamsky, Irina G. Voloshina, Artemiy D. Spitsyn
papers.summary: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff–that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. I(W;R) measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

papers.title: Beyond Source Code: Evaluating Natural Language Specifications for LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translation
papers.authors: Biruk Tadesse, Lawrence Arkoh, Marcelo D'Amorim, Wesley K. G. Assunção
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results for C-to-Rust translation, yet existing approaches primarily rely on source code as input, leaving natural-language specifications of program behavior underexplored as an alternative or complementary representation. We hypothesize that direct code translation encourages LLMs to preserve C-specific implementation choices, producing Rust that may be functionally correct but unnecessarily verbose, reliant on unsafe constructs, and less idiomatic.
